title: Sun Printing & Publishing Ass'n v. Remington Paper & Power Co.
lead: A newsprint buyer offers the maximum benchmark price after the seller refuses further deliveries, but the parties also left open how long each future price would last.

actors.name: Remington Paper & Power Company
actors.role: Seller contending that future pricing terms were incomplete.

actors.name: Canadian Export Paper Company
actors.role: Third-party supplier whose large-customer contract price supplied the ceiling.

proceedings: Special Term denied the buyer judgment on the pleadings.
The Appellate Division reversed and granted the motion.
The Court of Appeals reversed, restored the denial, and answered the certified sufficiency question negatively.
limits: The judgment addressed the complaint presented, leaving amendment and an unasserted refusal-to-negotiate theory open. It predates the UCC and does not decide how later sales law would govern.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Sun Printing and Remington fix quantities and the first four months’ prices
sections.cue: What did the writing leave for future agreement?
paragraphs: Sun Printing agreed to buy and Remington Paper & Power agreed to sell 1,000 tons of specified newsprint each month from September 1919 through December 1920, 16,000 tons overall. The writing specified quality and sizes and payment on the twentieth of each month for prior-month shipments. September’s price was $3.73¾ per hundred pounds; October through December carried a $4 price. Those four months were performed and paid.

For the remaining year, the parties promised to set both the price and how long it would govern fifteen days before each established period expired. A price ceiling used Canadian Export Paper Company’s contract rate to large customers, adjusted to give Remington the freight differential. That benchmark limited price but did not explicitly supply a future pricing period.

sections.title: Remington disclaims further obligation and Sun tenders at the benchmark
sections.cue: Why did the monthly demands become important?
paragraphs: Before the next agreement was due, Remington declared the arrangement incomplete and denied a duty to deliver more paper. Sun demanded 1,000 tons in each month of 1920 at the Canadian company’s then-current contract price, freight-adjusted, repeating the demand monthly until year’s end. It sued for nondelivery damages.

Market prices rose during 1920, making resistance to the ceiling economically understandable, but the majority later treated contractual undertaking rather than seller motive as decisive. Sun claimed that offering the highest permitted price completed the bargain. Remington answered that both price and duration required further assent and that it had granted no series of exclusive monthly options.

sections.title: The buyer wins in the intermediate court on its pleading motion
sections.cue: What facts had not been tried?
paragraphs: Special Term denied Sun’s motion for judgment on the pleadings. The Appellate Division reversed and granted it. Remington took a permitted appeal to the Court of Appeals, with the certified question whether the complaint stated sufficient facts for a cause of action.

This was not a trial determination of a reasonable price, duration, or settled trade practice. The dispute was whether the signed writing and allegations established the claimed delivery obligation, or whether deciding the unresolved pricing intervals would require a bargain the parties had yet to make.

sections.title: Cardozo distinguishes the amount of a price from the time it governs
sections.cue: How did the open period allocate market risk?
paragraphs: Judge Cardozo identified two reserved subjects. If only price were missing, the stated maximum might support a buyer’s option to require delivery at that figure. But finding a price at a moment did not determine its duration. The parties contemplated choosing a period, applying the Canadian benchmark at its start, and holding the resulting price through that period. Sun’s counsel conceded that the actual price was not agreed to rise and fall with every change in the benchmark.

A longer fixed period exposed Remington to a later benchmark increase and Sun to a later decrease. Duration therefore allocated risk and stability, rather than merely providing administrative convenience.

Sun argued that duration mattered only if the negotiated price was below the maximum. Cardozo found no such qualification in the writing. Sun also did not accept a binding commitment to the benchmark for the whole remaining year; it asserted an option exercised monthly. That construction put Remington at the buyer’s successive disposal without agreement to do so. Even one election for the entire quantity would not close the gap if the ceiling declined between shipments.

sections.title: The majority declines to write a monthly or reasonable period into this complaint
sections.cue: What potential additional allegations remained available?
paragraphs: The maximum addressed failure to agree on price, but the writing supplied no comparable answer for failure to agree on duration. Monthly periods, an automatically fluctuating price, or a reasonable term drawn from trade conditions could have been expressly chosen. In Cardozo’s view, adding one would alter the bargain, leaving the presented arrangement an agreement to agree for the remaining deliveries.

The complaint called the Canadian rate ascertainable. Some judges suggested that rate might actually have been fixed for the entire year, making duration immaterial. Sun had neither alleged nor argued that circumstance, and renewed monthly tenders implied a variable benchmark. If that understanding was wrong, amended allegations could correct it. The ruling was not a categorical finding that no future pleading could establish liability.

Cardozo also reserved whether arbitrary refusal to agree about duration might breach a duty if Sun offered to let Remington choose the periods. The complaint contained no such notice, negotiation-based claim, or willingness to proceed beyond Sun’s monthly construction. A demand carrying a condition Remington had no obligation to accept could not create liability for rejecting that demand.

sources.pinpoint: Majority holding and reservations; 235 N.Y. at 345–47

sections.title: Crane would preserve the evident commercial transaction through construction
sections.cue: Which alternatives did the dissent offer for the missing period?
paragraphs: Judge Crane, joined by Judge Hogan, would affirm Sun’s favorable pleading ruling. Sophisticated companies signed the seller’s detailed form, used binding purchase-and-sale language, fixed sixteen months of quantities, and performed four months. Declaring the remainder ineffective disregarded evident contractual intent where an intelligible benchmark existed.

Sun offered the maximum Remington could demand. Crane thought that supplied the missing economic term and that a seller refusing even to try further agreement should not benefit from its refusal. Duration could be supplied in several ways: the December Canadian rate could govern the year if evidence showed constancy; monthly shipments could support monthly pricing; the reference to a contract price could import the Canadian contracts’ own duration; or a reasonable period could be determined from trade and circumstances.

These were alternative constructions allowing the complaint and proof to proceed, not findings that the benchmark actually remained unchanged. Crane favored preserving documented commercial intent through gap filling; Cardozo insisted on assent to the particular risk allocation that selecting duration would create.

sections.title: The buyer loses its pleading judgment without a damages award to the seller
sections.cue: How narrowly should the result be stated?
paragraphs: Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Pound, McLaughlin, and Andrews joined Cardozo, making the decision five to two. The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division, affirmed Special Term’s denial of Sun’s motion, awarded the stated appellate costs, and answered the certified sufficiency question no.

It did not award Remington damages or decide a substitute supply agreement. The result concerns a pleaded price ceiling paired with an unresolved duration carrying material market risk. This was the court’s 1923 reasoning, before the Uniform Commercial Code, rather than a determination of how later sales legislation would treat the transaction.
